The rhythmic groups of 2, 3 and 4 beats
What disimos, trisimos and tetrasimos are

Phthongs are gathered into rhythmic groups. The red vertical bars mark where each group begins and ends. Depending on how many beats (counts) fit in one group, it is called disimos (2), trisimos (3) or tetrasimos (4) — and that many phthongs are said inside it.
Pick a group and tap ▶ to watch the pulse beat out the counts, over and over. Tap a beat to stop there.
Tap a steady beat with your hand and say the phthongs inside each group: \"1-2\" for disimos, \"1-2-3\" for trisimos, \"1-2-3-4\" for tetrasimos. Keep the pulse even.
Disimos: two phthongs between two red measure bars.
Trisimos: three phthongs between two red measure bars.
Tetrasimos: four phthongs between two red measure bars.
The marks that show how long a note lasts or stays silent
Time characters include the marks, which indicate how much time a pause or note adds to a note:
Heavy is timeless, without temporality, without tonality.
The fraction and a dot add a time to the punctuation marks, that is, to the equal, the little, the apostrophe, etc.
Yfen means that the note is played with small variations in its pitch.
Stitches are used when one phthong is joined to another. This is a smoother ascent with lighter intensity on the phthong.
The thrower is used when I want to do a more tonal ascent with a lot of intensity by nineting the phthong:
Trisimos means that for every 3 beats (or counts) 3 phthongs are said.
Tetrasimos means that for every 4 beats (or counts) 4 phthongs are said.
Varea is also used for a pause and is empty (we say nothing).
In one year we say two phongs are equal.
The gorgo divides the time in the phthongo that is also the previous one.
The present gorgo divides the time in the phthong it is on and divides it again.\nAlso from the side the dot is on it gives the time that was divided.
Quantity characters that raise the voice
Quantity characters show how many voices (phthongs) the melody rises. The “stronger” the character, the bigger the rise of the voice.
How much does the voice rise?
Pick a character and watch the voice climb the ladder.
Each character raises the voice by a set number of voices:
For bigger leaps we combine a base character (Oligon or Petasti) with embroideries and highs. Pick an interval to see how it is written.
Learn the simple characters first. The leaping ascents are just combinations of them — don’t be afraid of them!
Quantity characters that lower the voice
Quantity characters show how many voices (phthongs) the melody falls. The “heavier” the character, the bigger the drop of the voice.
How much does the voice fall?
Pick a character and watch the voice descend the ladder.
Each character lowers the voice by a set number of voices:
For bigger descents we combine the descending characters (slight, low…) into a single stacked neume. Pick an interval to see how it is written.
Learn the simple characters first. The leaping descents are just combinations of them — don’t be afraid of them!
The Yporroi is written as a single neume but is worth two apostrophes — a drop of two voices (-2).
The Psifiston is also called oxeia and is written below a note, and requires that note to be pronounced with liveliness or force, or higher.
Omalon is written below the phthong, usually the equal and the minor, and requires a smooth undulation of the voice up to the high voice.

The Syndesmos is called and another connects ascending phthongs with descending or equal, or equal to equal, without interrupting the voice.\nThe phthongs that are connected to each other do not accept two different syllables, but always one, which is placed in the first position.

The Endophone requires that we pronounce the phthong, under which it is, with the mouth closed, therefore weakly and through the nose.\nIf the phthong with the endophone also has a time point, the endophone also acts on the time point, so that all times of the phthong are recited through the nose.

Middle, acute and grave diapason; double diapason

The octachord system, the most useful of all, is also called diapason and heptaphony. It consists of eight phthongs, which form seven intervals. Thus the diatonic scale Pa Vou Ga Di Ke Zo Ni, which is repeated toward the acute and the grave with the same number of phthongs and the same proportion of intervals, is an octachord or diapason system.

In this system, the first phthong Pa of the middle diapason (6) corresponds and coincides with the eighth phthong Pa΄ of the acute diapason and likewise with the eighth phthong Pa of the grave diapason. The same applies proportionally to the remaining phthongs, and also to the intervals formed by the various phthongs of the scale.

In each scale of this system, the first phthong, which is the base of the scale (4), is at the same time the highest degree of the immediately graver scale. And the last phthong of each scale, which is its highest degree, is at the same time the base of the immediately more acute scale.

The parallage of the diatonic scale according to the diapason system is done in the ways set out in Part A. The diatonic testimonies according to this system are noted as nine (9).

It was called trochos because the teachers of music used, for the convenience of students, the shape of a wheel or circle, whose four diameters divided the circle into eight parts. On the basis of this figure, beginners were taught parallage in ascent and descent according to the pentachord system.

The pentachord system or trochos is a series of five phthongs, which form four intervals. For this reason the pentachord system is also called tetraphony. Among the Byzantines it is also called trochos (2).

According to this system we have a series of five phthongs, Pa, Vou, Ga, Di, Ke, which is repeated toward the acute and the grave with the same number of phthongs and exactly the same proportion of intervals. Therefore, in this case, we have repetition toward the acute and the grave of a five-phthong scale with four intervals.

In this system the higher phthong Ke is taken as the base (as Pa), so that we may begin a new similar pentachord in ascent with exactly the same intervals as the first pentachord. And the lower phthong Pa is taken as the higher phthong (as Ke), so that we may form a new similar pentachord in descent with exactly the same descending intervals as the first pentachord.

Therefore, the first phthong of this system coincides and corresponds exactly with the fifth, the ninth, the thirteenth, and so on, whether toward the acute or toward the grave. The same applies proportionally to the other phthongs.

In this system, the first pentachord (Pa, Vou, Ga, Di, Ke) agrees completely in intervals with the same first five phthongs (Pa, Vou, Ga, Di, Ke) of the octachord.

Thus in the diatonic scale according to the diapason, from Pa as base up to Vou΄, we have the following intervals in numerical form: 10 + 8 + 12 + 12 + 10 + 8 + 12 + 10. In the same scale according to trochos, from Pa through the first and second pentachord (Pa to Vou΄), we have the following intervals in numerical form: 10 + 8 + 12 + 12 and 10 + 8 + 12 + 12. Therefore the second pentachord differs in the last interval Pa΄-Vou΄, which according to the diapason is a lesser tone, while according to the pentachord it is a greater tone.

The difference becomes greater if we proceed toward the acute by yet another pentachord. According to the diapason, from Vou΄ we will have the pentachord Vou΄-Zo΄ with intervals 8 + 12 + 12 + 10, while according to trochos these same intervals will be as Pa, Vou, Ga, Di, Ke, that is 10 + 8 + 12 + 12.

Similarly, if from Pa we descend diatonically by five phthongs (Pa, Ni, Zo, Ke, Di), according to the diapason we will have intervals 12 + 8 + 10 + 12. According to trochos we descend from Pa as from Ke (Ke, Di, Ga, Vou, Pa), and therefore we have intervals 12 + 12 + 8 + 10.

Parallage according to the trochos system is done by intoning a series of five phthongs, of which the last becomes the beginning of a second similar series. In ascent: Pa, Vou, Ga, Di, (Ke/Pa), Vou, Ga, Di, (Ke/Pa), and so on. In descent: Ke, Di, Ga, Vou, (Pa/Ke), Di, Ga, Vou, (Pa/Ke), Di, Ga, Vou, and so on.

The testimonies of the phthongs according to this system agree every five. Thus the testimonies of the first diatonic pentachord in ascent (Pa, Vou, Ga, Di, Ke) agree with the testimonies of the second similar pentachord toward the acute (Ke, Zo, Ni, Pa΄, Vou΄). And the testimonies of the first diatonic pentachord in descent (Ke, Di, Ga, Vou, Pa) agree with the testimonies of the second similar pentachord toward the grave (Pa, Ni, Zo, Ke, Di).

Figure XVI shows, in comparison, the diatonic scales according to the diapason and according to trochos, with their intervals and testimonies.

How the compound ascending characters are written

A compound ascending character is a single written sign read as a combination of simpler neumes. Find the base first (Oligon, Ison or Apostrophos) — it sets the movement of the voice — then the small marks around it that add ornament or timing. The order they are read in is shown in the breakdown to the right of each composition.
On each line the compound character is on the left and the neumes that make it up are on the right. Tap a line to watch it break apart into its parts again.
Rises one voice — the basic ascent.
Stays on the same voice (a hold).
Descends one voice or gives an inflection.
Kentimata: ornament that lifts the voice.
Gorgon: the notes read fast, at half the time (½).
Digorgon: faster still — the notes at a quarter of the time (¼).
The gorgon is a small mark placed on a composition that makes its notes read fast — each in half the time (½).
The digorgon speeds things up even more: it splits the beat into smaller parts so the notes read at ¼ — the composition\'s total time stays the same.
The total time stays the same on both sides — it is just shared among more, faster parts.
Find the base first (Oligon / Ison / Apostrophos) — it sets the ascent — then look at the small marks that add ornament or timing. The order they are read in is shown in the breakdown to the right.
Oligon with kentimata above: rise one voice and ornament it with the kentimata.
The kentimata sit below-right: read as kentimata, then Oligon.
Oligon with an apostrophos and kentimata over the base.
Oligon with an ison and kentimata: ison (same voice) and kentimata.
The yporroi with a dot reads as ison, apostrophos and apostrophos with a fraction (a descending run).
With a gorgon: Oligon and kentimata, but in half the time.
Kentimata with a gorgon, then Oligon — double speed.
Ison and kentimata with a gorgon: the composition runs at ½ time.
Apostrophos and kentimata with a gorgon — fast ornament.
Yporroi with a gorgon: apostrophos with a gorgon and apostrophos, in half the time.
With a digorgon: ison, kentimata with a digorgon and Oligon — at ¼ of the time.
The signs that change the colour of a note

Quality signs do not move a note to a different pitch; they change how you sing it — its accent, liveliness, smoothness, timbre or a small waver in pitch. They sit above, below or beside a note and give it character.
All eight quality signs at a glance:
Base neumes used in the examples
The same base neume (ison, oligon, apostrophe) sounds different depending on the quality sign next to it. Learn the base first, then “colour” it with the quality.
Close your mouth slightly and let the sound out through your nose — a soft, nasal “mmm”. If the note also has a time sign, its whole duration is sung this way.
An example where a continuous elaphron is NOT performed, because the syllable changes and there is a fraction over the apostrophe.
Without a Vareia: ison, apostrophe with a gorgon and oligon — all with the same liveliness.
With a Vareia in front, the ison takes a heavy accent and stands out from its neighbouring notes.
In front of one, two or more dots the Vareia no longer binds; it becomes a pause of as many beats.
Ison with a fraction = two isons joined by one yfen.
Ison with two dots = three isons joined by two yfen.
Continuous elaphron = apostrophe with a gorgon and apostrophe, almost glued together.
With an ison in front: ison, then apostrophe with a gorgon and apostrophe.
The psifiston under the first note makes it livelier than the two that follow.
On the kentimata the psifiston gives a livelier delivery.
Oligon with an omalon: oligon, kentimata with a gorgon and apostrophe — a smooth wave of the voice.
Under three notes the omalon’s energy spreads across all three.
Antikenoma under an oligon, with an apostrophe following — a small flick of the voice.
Bound to a single dot, it acts between the first and second beat of the note.
The syndesmos joins two isons into one syllable, without breaking the voice.
It likewise joins an oligon and an ison into one syllable.
